intro: Marcelle Meyer plays Rameau’s gavotte and six variations on the piano. A measured dance becomes a workout for the fingers, with quick runs passing from one hand to the other.

sections.label: Theme · The gavotte in A minor
sections.mNote: Two repeated halves, with trills and little turns

sections.label: Var 1 · The right hand runs
sections.mNote: Quick upper notes surround the slower left-hand tune

sections.label: Var 2 · The left hand answers
sections.mNote: Running bass notes support the upper chords

sections.label: Var 3 · A moving middle voice
sections.mNote: Quick notes move between the held outer parts

sections.label: Var 4 · Repeated notes in pairs
sections.mNote: Two quick strikes on each note animate the tune

sections.label: Var 5 · Leaps in the right hand
sections.mNote: The upper part jumps between low and high notes

sections.label: Var 6 · Leaps in the left hand
sections.mNote: The bass takes the running figures to the final cadence

relations.label: The gavotte’s second strain repeats
relations.basis: The gavotte has two repeated strains, the second twice the length of the first. These excerpts lie in that longer strain and its repeat before the first double. CENS diagonal mean 0.957, sustained 25 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The first double repeats its second strain
relations.basis: The first double retains the gavotte’s repeated-strain design while adding upper figuration. These excerpts compare the same strain within that double. CENS diagonal mean 0.975, sustained 16.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 19 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The harmonic route survives another double
relations.basis: The fifth and sixth doubles preserve the gavotte’s harmonic route while changing the keyboard figuration. The long paired excerpts lie in their later strains; the relation does not claim identical melody or finger-work. CENS diagonal mean 0.929, sustained 26.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 50 s (cache/form/rameau-gavotte-six-doubles.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A dance in two halves
cues.text: The gavotte moves in two broad beats, with trills and small turns decorating its tune. Each half repeats. Rameau keeps these phrases and their cadences through six doubles — variations that give the fingers steadily more to do.
cues.evidence: Rameau, Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin, Saint-Saëns edition (Durand, 1895), pp. 76–81: gavotte and six doubles. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An organist moves to Paris
cues.text: In 1722, Rameau moves from Clermont to Paris and publishes his Traité de l’harmonie. He already has years of church organ playing behind him. His first opera at the Paris Opéra, Hippolyte et Aricie, follows in 1733, when he is fifty.
cues.evidence: M. Elizabeth C. Bartlet, Rameau biography in Europe, 1450 to 1789: Encyclopedia of the Early Modern World, on Clermont, Paris, the 1722 treatise and the 1733 Opéra début. https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/music-history-composers-and-performers-biographies/jean-philippe-rameau-0

cues.title: The right hand starts running
cues.text: The first double sets a continuous stream of semiquavers above a slower tune in the left hand. The gavotte’s chords still arrive at their familiar places, but the right hand now fills the spaces between them.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 76–77, first double: continuous upper semiquavers and slower left-hand notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Now the left hand runs
cues.text: The second double turns the arrangement upside down. The left hand takes the semiquavers, climbing through broken chords, while the right hand holds the slower notes. The busy part of the piano has moved below the tune.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 77, second double: running left-hand semiquavers beneath sustained upper chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A voice between the others
cues.text: The third double puts quick notes inside the chords. A held upper note and a slower bass surround the moving middle voice. The piano seems to have more than two hands at work.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 78, third double: sustained outer notes around the moving inner part.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two strikes on one note
cues.text: The fourth double makes the pianist repeat notes in quick pairs before moving on. The tune bounces from one pair to the next, with a few running figures breaking through. Rameau keeps the gavotte’s two broad beats underneath.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 78–79, fourth double: paired repeated semiquavers within the unchanged duple metre.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The right hand leaps
cues.text: The fifth double sends the right hand jumping between separated notes. Short runs bridge the gaps, while slower bass notes keep the dance grounded. The same A minor phrases now demand a much wider reach.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 79–80, fifth double: separated upper notes joined by semiquavers, over a slower bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass has the last word
cues.text: The sixth double gives the running figures to the left hand beneath held right-hand chords. Low and high notes alternate within the bass line. The whole set ends with this variation’s cadence in A minor.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, pp. 80–81, sixth double: left-hand running figures and the final A minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Semiquavers fill the dance’s spaces
transitions.from: Theme · The gavotte in A minor
transitions.how: The gavotte closes in A minor. The first double begins the same phrases with continuous right-hand semiquavers above slower left-hand notes. On Meyer’s piano, the tune now sits beneath the running part; the two-beat dance continues.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 76: the gavotte’s A minor cadence and the first double’s upper semiquavers. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

transitions.title: The flowing line breaks into pairs
transitions.how: The third double completes its A minor cadence. The fourth restarts the dance with pairs of repeated notes, each pair nudging the tune onwards. The moving inner voice has become a succession of quick repeated strikes above the bass.
transitions.evidence: Saint-Saëns edition, p. 78: third-double cadence and the opening paired notes of the fourth double. https://archive.org/download/imslp-suites-de-pices-de-clavecin-rameau-jean-philippe/Rameau_-_nouvelles_suite.pdf

composer.epithet: He explained the roots of chords in a treatise, then sent them through hell in his first opera, at fifty.
facts: Organist in Dijon, Clermont-Ferrand and Lyon; first harpsichord book, 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
Alexandre Le Riche de La Pouplinière, financier with a private orchestra
composer.background:
When Hippolyte et Aricie opened at the Paris Opéra on 1 October 1733, Rameau had just turned fifty. The singers and players had already defeated one of its boldest pages: a trio for the Fates whose lurching harmonies proved too difficult in rehearsal and had to be cut. The rest was quite enough to divide the house. Admirers heard a new theatrical voice; devotees of Lully heard an attack on their inheritance. An organist from Dijon had arrived with a first opera and a great deal of music to get off his chest.

His father played the organ in Dijon. Jean-Philippe followed the trade through a succession of French churches, with appointments in Clermont-Ferrand, Dijon and Lyon and an early attempt to establish himself in Paris. There he published his first harpsichord book in 1706. It begins with an unmeasured prelude: notes whose timing the player must work out, followed by a faster section that suddenly acquires a regular beat. Allemandes, courante and sarabandes follow. He was twenty-three, writing within the French keyboard tradition before Couperin had published his first book.
